Wildlife Detection Capstone: Results Notebook¶

Regenerates every figure and table in the report from the saved run data in data/. Figures are written to figures/. All detection scores are on the validation set (180 images, 629 boxes) unless stated; the held-out test set has not been used yet. Each configuration was trained with 3 seeds (0, 1, 2); ± is the sample standard deviation across seeds.

Config What it is
S0 YOLOv8n fine-tuned, every augmentation switched off
S1 S0 + standard augmentation (mosaic, colour jitter, translate, scale, flip, mixup 0.1)
S2 (void) S1 + Ultralytics built-in copy_paste=0.3. Does nothing on box-only data, so it is identical to S1 and is not plotted
S2sam S1 + 400 synthetic training images made by pasting SAM-masked elephants, birds and antelope
S3rfs S1 + repeat-factor sampling (rare-class images appear more often per epoch)
S3w S1 + class-weighted classification loss
S4 S1 + 38 pseudo-labelled frames from new videos (leak-checked)
In [1]:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, matplotlib.image as mpimg
from pathlib import Path
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 10})
D, F = Path("data"), Path("figures"); F.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
CLASSES = ["antelope","bird","chimpanzee","elephant","gorilla","hippo","hog"]
CFG = ["S0","S1","S2sam","S3rfs","S3w","S4"]; COL = {"S0":"#8c8c8c","S1":"#2a6fbb","S2sam":"#d9822b","S3rfs":"#4c9a6a","S3w":"#8e5ea2","S4":"#b5534b"}
res = pd.read_csv(D/"results_val_per_seed.csv")
print(res.groupby("config").size().to_dict(), "rows per config (3 seeds x 8 rows)")

{'S0': 24, 'S1': 24, 'S2sam': 24, 'S3rfs': 24, 'S3w': 24, 'S4': 24} rows per config (3 seeds x 8 rows)

1. The dataset and the split problem¶

Nine recording sessions, 3,909 boxes, 7 classes. Elephant has only 131 boxes; hippo and chimpanzee together are 61% of all boxes.

In [2]:
counts = pd.Series({"hippo":1219,"chimpanzee":1163,"hog":421,"bird":379,"antelope":347,"gorilla":249,"elephant":131})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,3.2))
ax.barh(counts.index[::-1], counts.values[::-1], color="#2a6fbb")
for i,v in enumerate(counts.values[::-1]): ax.text(v+10, i, f"{v}  ({v/3909:.1%})", va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("Bounding boxes"); ax.set_title("Class balance (all 3,909 boxes)"); ax.set_xlim(0,1500)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(F/"01_class_balance.png"); plt.show()

1.1 Chimpanzee: the old split tested on a different kind of footage¶

The chimpanzee video switches from normal widescreen footage to portrait phone footage padded with blurred side bars. A chronological split put only the padded, distant footage in validation and test. The fix split the video into two formats, cropped the bars off, and split each format separately.

In [3]:
sh = pd.read_csv(D/"shift_stats.csv")
old = sh[(sh.dataset=="wildlife-yolo-naive") & (sh["class"]=="chimpanzee")].groupby("split").median_area_pct.first()
new = sh[(sh.dataset=="wildlife-yolo") & (sh["class"]=="chimpanzee")].pivot_table(index="split", columns="unit", values="median_area_pct")
order = ["train","val","test"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(9,3.3), sharey=True)
ax[0].bar(order, [old[s] for s in order], color="#b04a4a"); ax[0].set_title("Old split: one chimp video, cut in time")
w=0.38; x=np.arange(3)
ax[1].bar(x-w/2, [new.loc[s,"chimpanzees_land"] for s in order], w, label="widescreen part", color="#2a6fbb")
ax[1].bar(x+w/2, [new.loc[s,"chimpanzees_port"] for s in order], w, label="portrait part (bars cropped)", color="#d9822b")
ax[1].set_xticks(x); ax[1].set_xticklabels(order); ax[1].set_title("Fixed split: each format split separately"); ax[1].set_ylim(0, 7.4); ax[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper center", fontsize=8, ncol=1)
ax[0].set_ylabel("Median chimp box (% of image area)")
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(F/"02_chimp_split_fix.png"); plt.show()
print("Old split: train", round(old['train'],2), "% vs val", round(old['val'],2), "% / test", round(old['test'],2), "%")

1.1b Matched check: is the chimpanzee jump caused by the split? (old split, same S0 settings)¶

Three seeds trained on the OLD split with augmentation off (exactly the S0 settings), then scored on both the old and the fixed evaluation sets.

# Which differences are bigger than seed noise?  Welch t-statistic over 3 seeds; |t|>2.8 is roughly p<0.05 at ~4 d.o.f.
from math import sqrt
def welch(a,b):
    return (b.mean()-a.mean())/sqrt(a.var(ddof=1)/len(a)+b.var(ddof=1)/len(b))
out=[]
for pair in [("S0","S1")]+[("S1",c) for c in CFG[2:]]:
    for k in ["all"]+CLASSES:
        for metric in ["mAP50","mAP50-95","recall"]:
            a=res[(res.config==pair[0])&(res["class"]==k)][metric]; b=res[(res.config==pair[1])&(res["class"]==k)][metric]
            t=welch(a,b); out.append([f"{pair[0]} -> {pair[1]}",k,metric,b.mean()-a.mean(),t,abs(t)>2.8])
sig=pd.DataFrame(out,columns=["comparison","class","metric","change","t","beyond_noise"])
sig.to_csv(F/"table_significance.csv",index=False)
print("Differences beyond seed noise (|t| > 2.8, 3 seeds; indicative only, not a formal test):")
sig[sig.beyond_noise].round(3).sort_values(["comparison","metric"])

Differences beyond seed noise (|t| > 2.8, 3 seeds; indicative only, not a formal test):

5. Confusion matrices¶

Read the threshold first. Ultralytics draws confusion matrices at the validation confidence threshold, which defaults to 0.001. At that setting thousands of near-zero-confidence boxes are counted, so the matrices show species mix-ups and false alarms that do not happen at a working threshold. The first figure (validation set, saved during training) is at 0.001 and is kept only for completeness. The second figure (test set) is drawn at confidence 0.25 and is the one to read.

6c. Experiment A: holding out whole recording sessions¶

Models trained on gorillas, gorillas2 and hippo2 only; tested on the unseen sessions gorillas3 and hippo. The default-split column uses different test images and far more training data, so the comparison shows the size of the problem, not a precise gap.

6d. External check on new footage (4 videos, one known species each)¶

Share of frames whose top detection is the video's species. Species recognition only, not box accuracy; S4 is excluded because its training used frames from these videos.

7. Reading the results (plain English)¶

  • Fixing the split mattered most for chimpanzee (validation mAP50 0.09 to about 0.67; about 0.78 on test). The old-split run also differed in augmentation and stopping, but the jump is far beyond what those could explain.
  • Standard augmentation (S1) is the clear winner: overall mAP50 +0.075 on validation and +0.10 on test, mostly for classes that were thin or shifted (elephant, antelope, hippo).
  • Built-in copy-paste cannot run on box-only data (it reproduced S1 exactly). SAM copy-paste (S2sam) raises bird recall on validation and does best on new elephant footage, but is not a net gain on test.
  • Class-imbalance remedies (S3) and pseudo-labelling (S4) gave no clear gain. Pseudo-labelling was limited because the model is not confident on unfamiliar footage, so only 38 frames qualified.
  • Bird remains essentially undetected on the test set for every configuration.
  • The headline risk is cross-session generalisation. Holding out whole sessions drops gorilla and hippo test mAP50 to about 0.15 and 0.06, and models identify the right species in only a fraction of frames of new videos. Validation and chronological test scores are optimistic for single-session classes.
  • Deployment: the ONNX model is 12 MB, matches PyTorch accuracy within 0.003 mAP50, and runs at about 13 ms per image on this PC's CPU (not a field device).
  • Caveats: 3 seeds; a 180-image validation set; elephant has 18 validation boxes; many comparisons were made, so a few flagged differences will be chance; the external check uses video-level labels and correlated frames; Experiment A compares different test images and training sizes.
